text: Katherine Stoneman (April 1841 – May 19, 1925) was an early 20th-century suffragist and the first woman admitted to the Bar Association in the State of New York. Born on her family's farm in Busti, Chautauqua County, New York, she was the fifth of eight children; her family operated in the lumber business, and her father served as a justice of the peace for several years. One of her brothers, George Stoneman, became the Governor of California, and her brother Edward served as a Judge on the Supreme Court of Illinois. In 1864, she began attending the Albany Normal School to become a teacher, where she also worked as a copyist for the New York Court of Appeals. She graduated from Albany Law School of Union University, founded in 1851, in 1866 and began teaching at the Glens Falls Seminary, later teaching at her alma mater, the Albany Normal School. She served as the first female president of their alumni association and as Vice-Principal. In 1885, Stoneman became the first woman to pass the New York Bar Exam, but her application to the bar was rejected in the spring of 1886 due to her gender. With support from local suffragettes, she advocated for a bill allowing admission of all qualified applicants regardless of race or gender. The bill was introduced, passed, and signed by Governor David Hill on May 20, 1886, just nine days after her rejection. Twelve years after her bar admission, she returned to study law formally at Albany Law School, where she became the first woman to graduate in 1898. She maintained a law office in Albany from 1889 to 1922. She died on May 19, 1925, and is buried in Albany Rural Cemetery. Stoneman was inducted into the National Women's Hall of Fame in October 2009. The eponymous Kate Stoneman Project celebrates and advances women in the legal profession.
